title: Comparison
tagline: Not just faster or fastest: how much faster, faster than what, and what keeps rising together.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Reading & Use of English Part 3 — word formation
why: At B2, comparison is more than -er and -est: it's about how much bigger a difference is (slightly, far, by far), comparing equal things (as...as), and structures like the more..., the better that don't exist in most other languages. Part 4 regularly tests these modifiers and fixed patterns, and Speaking Part 2 depends on them for comparing two photos naturally.

diagrams.title: the + comparative, the + comparative
diagrams.caption: The more you practise, the better you get.

rows.label: Meaning
cells: in the role of; in the same way that

rows.label: Example

head: Pattern
Use
Example
rows: one syllable, or two ending in -y
better / best; worse / worst; further / furthest
much / a lot / far / slightly / a bit + -er
by far the fastest runner in the year
as fast as; not as fast as
twice as expensive as the other one
two things increasing or decreasing together
The sooner we leave, the better.

examples.text: Cusco is higher than Lima, so the air feels thinner.
Chemistry is more demanding than most subjects, in Liam's opinion.
This is the most exciting match we've played all season.

use.point: Modifiers: how big is the difference?

examples.text: Sofia's score was only slightly higher than Nadia's.
The new stadium is far bigger than the old one.
Mateo is by far the fastest swimmer in the school.
This year's team isn't as strong as last year's.
The coast route is twice as long as the mountain route.
Her Spanish is now almost as fluent as her English.

use.point: Parallel increase, and like vs as

examples.text: The more Nadia trains, the more confident she feels before a race.
Sofia plays the guitar like a professional musician.
As the team captain, Mateo has to arrive before everyone else.

watch_out.wrong: This exam was more difficult that the last one.
watch_out.right: This exam was more difficult than the last one.
watch_out.why: Comparatives are followed by than, not that.

watch_out.wrong: She's the more intelligent student in the class.
watch_out.right: She's the most intelligent student in the class.
watch_out.why: Comparing one person with a whole group needs a superlative, not a comparative.

watch_out.wrong: This bag is very bigger than mine.
watch_out.right: This bag is much / far / a lot bigger than mine.
watch_out.why: Very cannot modify a comparative; use much, a lot, far or slightly instead.

watch_out.wrong: He is as older as his brother.
watch_out.right: He is as old as his brother.
watch_out.why: As...as uses the base adjective, never the comparative form.

watch_out.wrong: Miss Vega talks as a native speaker.
watch_out.right: Miss Vega talks like a native speaker.
watch_out.why: Comparing two things (similarity) needs like + noun, not as.

watch_out.wrong: The harder you train, more you improve.
watch_out.right: The harder you train, the more you improve.
watch_out.why: Both halves of this pattern need 'the' before the comparative.

dialogue.title: Choosing a new football boot
dialogue.context: Liam and Mateo are comparing two pairs of football boots before Liam buys new ones, with Nadia giving her opinion.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: These are lighter than my old ones, but they're also far more expensive.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: The blue ones look slightly better for grip, though. Which pitch do you play on most?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: The school field — it's not as smooth as the club pitch.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Then get the ones with more studs. The rougher the ground, the more grip you need.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: True. These red ones are by far the most popular with the team, by the way.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Popular doesn't mean better, though. My last pair felt like running in cardboard.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: As your best friend, I'd say get the ones that actually fit properly.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Fair point. Try them on — the sooner you decide, the sooner we can leave.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: These blue ones are twice as comfortable as the red pair, honestly.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Done, then. They were also a lot cheaper than I expected.

items.sentence: Arequipa is much ___ than Lima in July.
This is ___ exciting film I've seen all year.
items.why: superlative for one thing compared to a whole group

items.sentence: Her grades are ___ as good as they were last term.
items.why: not as ... as for an unequal comparison

items.sentence: The new bridge is ___ longer than the old one — almost double the length.
He plays the piano ___ a professional, even though he's only fifteen.
The ___ you leave, the more traffic you'll hit.
Mateo is ___ the fastest runner in his year group.

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct comparative or superlative form of the word in brackets.

items.sentence: This year's science fair was ___ (good) than last year's by far.
Sofia is ___ (organised) student in the whole class.
The mountain route is ___ (far) than the coast road.
This laptop is ___ (expensive) than the one I wanted.
The bus wasn't ___ (crowded) as we expected.
The new stadium holds ___ (many) people as the old one.
The ___ (early) you book, the cheaper the tickets are.
Of all the players, Nadia trains ___ (hard).

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.first: No other student in the year is as tall as Liam.
Sofia's essay was a little better than Mateo's.
This year's exam was much harder than last year's.
As you practise more, you get more confident.
Nadia's bag costs double what mine cost.
Liam is not as confident as his sister.

summary: Short adjectives take -er/-est; longer adjectives take more/most; good, bad and far are irregular.
Modifiers show the size of the difference: slightly/a bit (small), much/a lot/far (big), by far/easily (with superlatives).
As...as compares equal things and always uses the base adjective, never the comparative.
The + comparative, the + comparative links two things that rise or fall together.
Like compares two similar things (+ noun); as talks about a role or the way something is done (+ clause or noun).
